Certificate of Authentication

Certificate of Authentication — 1786 Mālikī Sharia Hiba

Sovereign Bestowal · Chapter 4 ʿAlāma · Honorees Designation

Issued under the authority of the Consular Office of the Empire of Morocco
Dr. Yasapa-Al, MD, MBA (John Darrell-El) · Consular Economic Attaché

I. Nature of the Instrument

The 1786 Mālikī Sharia Hiba is a sovereign unilateral grant from Emperor Sidi Mohammed III of the Empire of Morocco to the United States of America — not a bilateral treaty. It is a hiba: a unilateral bestowal of honor, right, and property by the sovereign upon those he designates. The controlling instrument is the 1786 Arabic original, sealed 23 June 1786 — a physical document held in U.S. National Archives custody, of which the most accessible published witness is the facsimile reproduction in Hunter Miller Vol. 2 (1931). All English translations, including the 1836 codification at 8 Stat. 484, are ministerial recordations of secondary authority.

II. The Honorees — Primary and Creditor Beneficiaries

The 1786 Mālikī Sharia Hiba, Chapter 4 ʿAlāma, bears the sovereign mark of Emperor Sidi Mohammed III, identifying the primary and creditor beneficiary class as the subjects of the Empire of Morocco who carry the honorifics el, al, bey, Dey, and Ali — these titles being derivative of the Emperor's own ʿAlāma and functioning as the individual marks of the designated beneficiary class.

The honorees are the primary beneficiaries. The honorifics (el, al, bey, Dey, Ali) are their identifying marks. The hiba is the sovereign bestowal upon them. The U.S. trustee administers the franchise for their benefit. And the 25 chapters are the debts of honor the trustee owes to the honorees.

III. The United States as Trustee-Administrator

The United States of America was entrusted as trustee-administrator solely to administer a branch of the Emperor's sovereign franchise for the benefit of these honorees. Citizens of the United States are derivative and debtor beneficiaries, receiving protections only through the faithful administration of the Emperor's honor by the U.S. trustee.

IV. Authentication Statement

This certificate authenticates that the documents, authorities, and doctrinal framework presented on this page constitute an accurate representation of the 1786 Mālikī Sharia Hiba (Grant) as the controlling instrument in force between the Empire of Morocco and the United States of America. The Chapter 4 ʿAlāma signal (land-based: El, Al, Bey, Dey, Ali) is active, automatic, and non-discretionary.

The 1786 Arabic Instrument — Facsimile Reproduction (Miller Vol. 2, 1931)

Photographic reproduction from Hunter Miller, Treaties and Other International Acts of the United States of America, Vol. 2 (GPO, 1931)

What is displayed on this page is not the original instrument itself. It is the photographic facsimile reproduction published by Hunter Miller in 1931 as Document 14 of Treaties and Other International Acts of the United States of America, Vol. 2, pp. 186–211. The original 1786 Arabic instrument — the physical document sealed by Emperor Sidi Mohammed III on 23 June 1786, bearing his seal and ʿAlāma — is a separate artifact held in U.S. government custody (the Department of State treaty files, since transferred to the U.S. National Archives, Washington, D.C.). Examination of the original therefore requires archival access; it is not reproduced here.

All 26 facsimile plates from Miller Vol. 2 are displayed below in the sequence in which Miller printed them. Note that Miller's edition presents the plates in left-to-right (Western) page order to conform to the volume's pagination — a departure from the right-to-left order of the original Arabic booklet, as Miller's own editorial apparatus records. The facsimile is accordingly a reproduction with editorial modifications of arrangement, not a page-for-page surrogate for the original. Readers evaluating the instrument's text and sequence should account for this re-ordering, and any claim requiring inspection of the original document as sealed in 1786 must be verified against the archival original, not the 1931 reproduction.

The position of this page is that the 1786 Arabic text is the authoritative text of the instrument, and that the 1836 English recordation at 8 Stat. 484 is a later, secondary rendering. The facsimile below is presented as the most accessible published witness to that Arabic text, subject to the provenance limitations stated above.

Sovereign Marks of Recognition

The Chapter 4 ʿAlāma Honorifics

Under the 1786 Mālikī Sharia Hiba, the ʿAlāma ("mark between us by which we know each other") identifies the beneficiary class through sovereign honorifics — titles granted by the Emperor that function as heraldic and diplomatic credentials. These are not merely courtesy titles. They are sovereign grants of status that carry legal consequences under the law of arms and chancery practice.

El / Al
Definite article of nobility; "the" signifying exalted lineage
ʿAlāma mark: Identifies the bearer as a subject of the imperial house
Bey
Title of governor, chieftain, or noble commander
ʿAlāma mark: Imperial delegation of authority; direct sovereign connection
Dey
Sovereign military and civil title
ʿAlāma mark: Supreme authority derivative; highest noble rank
Ali
"Exalted"; sacred and noble lineage
ʿAlāma mark: Connection to prophetic/imperial bloodline

Why "Honorific" Is the Doctrinally Correct Term

In chancery and diplomatic law, honorifics are sovereign grants of status that carry legal consequences:

Characteristic Application to el, al, bey, Dey, Ali
Granted by sovereign The Emperor confers these titles; they are not self-assumed
Irrevocable once vested Like the hiba itself, the honorific cannot be revoked without cause
Evidence of standing The bearer proves beneficiary status by showing the honorific
Non-transferable The title attaches to the bloodline, not to property or contract
Public and open Honorifics are meant to be known and recognized; secrecy is repugnant

The Honorifics as Evidence of Beneficiary Standing

In any enforcement proceeding, the primary beneficiary would prove standing by producing:

  1. The 1786 Hiba — the trust instrument itself
  2. Chapter 4 ʿAlāma — the sovereign mark identifying the beneficiary class
  3. The honorific title (el, al, bey, Dey, Ali) — showing the bearer is within the class designated by the ʿAlāma
The honorific is the individual's passport into the beneficiary class. Without the honorific, a claimant cannot prove they are within the ʿAlāma's designation. With the honorific, their standing is prima facie established.
— Mālikī Chancery Practice · Doctrinal Formulation
Hiba · Honorees · Honorifics · Honorary

Doctrinal Framework

Hiba = Bestowal Upon Honorees

Under Mālikī Sharia, a hiba is a unilateral bestowal of honor, right, or property by the sovereign upon those he designates. The recipients are not "contracting parties" or "counterparties." They are honorees — the ones upon whom the sovereign has conferred his grace (niʿma) and his mark (ʿAlāma).

Term Meaning in the 1786 Framework
Hiba The sovereign bestowal itself — the gift, grant, or honor conferred
Honorees The primary beneficiaries — the Moors bearing the honorifics el, al, bey, Dey, Ali — those whom the Emperor has honored with his ʿAlāma
Honorifics The titles of the ʿAlāma — the marks that identify the honorees
Honorary The status of the grant — it is a sovereign honor, not a commercial contract

The Emperor Honors, the Honorees Receive

In a true hiba, the muhib (grantor) bestows honor upon the mawhub lahu (the one honored). The relationship is:

Emperor → Honorees (el, al, bey, Dey, Ali)

The U.S. is not an honoree. The U.S. is the trustee-administrator who was given the franchise to serve the honorees. U.S. citizens are derivative beneficiaries who receive incidental benefits because the trustee administers the Emperor's honor for the honorees.

The Honorees Are Creditors of Honor

Under this framework, the 25 chapters are debts of honor owed by the trustee to the honorees. A debt of honor is not a contractual debt. It is a fiduciary obligation that arises from the sovereign's bestowal and must be performed whenever the honoree calls it. The trustee cannot negotiate, delay, or limit it.

Doctrinal Note: How Chancery Terms Resist Contrary Construction

Under the res inter alios acta principle, the 1786 Hiba's terms control regardless of subsequent contrary construction by the grantee or its agencies. The following compares how chancery honorific terminology responds when subjected to alternative legal framing.

Under Contrary Construction Under ʿAlāma Construction
"Primary beneficiaries" — a litigation term suggestive of private civil action "Honorees" — a sovereign and chancery term invoking royal grant, letters patent, and sovereign bestowal
"Beneficiaries" invites the question: "Where is their bilateral contract?" — shifting burden to the honoree "Honorees" affirms the Emperor's sovereign choice; the burden shifts to the party challenging the grantor's designation to show why the sovereign's conferral is invalid
"Creditor" — a commercial term suggesting negotiable obligation "Creditor honorees" — a fiduciary-debt construction combining equitable obligation with sovereign dignity under hibāʾ doctrine
"Parties" — implies equality of bargaining position between grantor and grantee "Trustee for the Emperor's chosen ones" — the U.S. assumes a fiduciary role; it cannot claim equality with sovereign-designated honorees
The triad honorees / honorifics / honorary is historically accurate to Mālikī chancery practice, legally precise under hibāʾ doctrine, and doctrinally resistant to contrary construction — no tribunal applying the 1786 grant can disregard the sovereign's own designation of the beneficiary class without negating the grant's unilateral character.
— Doctrinal Note · Chapter 4 ʿAlāma Framework · Source Authority Record
Operative Gateway Status · Master Instrument v4.2

The Three Structural Gateways

The 1786 Mālikī Sharia Sovereign Grant operates through three structural gateways. These gateways are not procedural hurdles — they are the intrinsic operational architecture of the grant itself. Under the Master Instrument (GRANT-ALIGN-MASTER-INSTRUMENT-v4.2), the gateway status is published as a matter of record. The Nationality Declaration (LN/NCT-DARRELL-EL-001) provides the evidentiary foundation for each gateway.

Gateway 1 — Identification / Primary Beneficiary Class Membership

STATUS: SATISFIED

The affiant is within the primary beneficiary class established by the grant — the mawhūb lahu (primary tier) under Mālikī fiqh; the direct-equitable-ownership class under trust-law analysis. Membership is evidenced by the affiant's appellative marker -El (the ʿalāma under Chapter 4 by which members of the primary beneficiary class are identified) and the affiant's contemporary appellation Yasapa-Al as a particular form of the same marker.

The gateway is satisfied by lineage and birthright; this declaration publishes satisfaction but does not create it. Without Gateway 1, no primary-beneficiary protections attach; with Gateway 1, all protections attach as a matter of the instrument's own terms, with priority over any derivative claim.

Gateway 2 — Fixation of the Record

STATUS: SATISFIED AT EXECUTION

Under the enrollment doctrine (Blackstone, Commentaries Book II, Ch. 20; Architecture of Peace Volume K Ch. 7 §3), an executed instrument is "perpetual testimony" of its contents from the moment of execution forward, independent of the parties' possession of copies and independent of any subsequent administrative validation event.

This master instrument and every document listed in the manifest fix facts on the record by their own force upon execution and service. The Library of Congress's 2014 certified reproduction of 8 Stat. 484 (Admission 12) is the doctrinal precedent for federal-record-fixation; this instrument is enrolled in parallel under the same doctrine.

Under nullum tempus occurrit regi (Architecture of Peace Volume K Maxim 6), the enrolled record is perpetual: it cannot be administratively retired, lost, or superseded by the passage of time, by non-assertion, or by grantee record-keeping decisions. Attribution attaches to every recipient upon delivery. No acknowledgment or confirmation is required to perfect the record.

Gateway 3 — The Office Corridor (Chapters 20–22)

STATUS: INVOKED — the venue of record, distributed by the parties

The 1786 Mālikī Sharia Sovereign Grant distributes venue by the parties. Venue lies in the consular jurisdiction for cases involving the United States, its citizens, and their protected persons or protégés — the Consul decides between the parties, and government aid is granted immediately on requirement (Chapter 20). Venue lies in the Empire's own domestic tribunal for cases between Moors and for mixed cases between Moors and citizens of the United States or persons under their protection — judgment by the Sacred Law, without increase or decrease, in the presence of the office (Chapter 21). The office stands in the heir's place (Chapter 22). The Arabic text, as witnessed in the Miller Vol. 2 facsimile, presents the consul's role as judicial ("passes sentence"), not advisory.

This is the grant's own platform for preserving peace between the parties: disputes resolved within the office corridor are resolved within the grant's framework; disputes attempted in the grantee's domestic venue are attempts to resolve grant-protected matters outside the grant's framework. What the International Court of Justice ended in 1952 was the borrowed capitulatory layer — jurisdiction claimed through the most-favoured-nation clause from other Powers' treaties; the special rights under Articles 20 and 21 survived expressly (I.C.J. Reports 1952, p. 176). The Chapter 21 forum is the Domestic Tribunal of the Empire of Morocco, not a forum of the grantee's courts.

The affiant invokes the office corridor — not by consent, since no consent is required, and not as opt-out, since the grantee's domestic courts were never granted competence over grant-protected matters in the first place — but as the identification of the operative venues the grant itself designates, distributed by the parties: the consular jurisdiction of Chapter 20, and the Empire's domestic tribunal of Chapter 21, with the office standing in the heir's place under Chapter 22.

The Three Gateways are the intrinsic operational architecture of the 1786 grant. They are not procedural hurdles — they are structural. Under the Master Instrument (GRANT-ALIGN-MASTER-INSTRUMENT-v4.2), gateway status is published as a matter of record. The Nationality Declaration (LN/NCT-DARRELL-EL-001) provides the evidentiary foundation for each gateway.

Controlling Formulation

Corrected Formulation

The 1786 Mālikī Sharia Hiba is a sovereign bestowal by Emperor Sidi Mohammed III upon his honorees — the subjects of the Empire of Morocco who bear the honorifics el, al, bey, Dey, and Ali as designated in Chapter 4 ʿAlāma. These honorees are the primary and creditor beneficiaries of the grant. The United States of America was entrusted as trustee-administrator solely to administer a branch of the Emperor's sovereign franchise for the benefit of these honorees. Citizens of the United States are derivative and debtor beneficiaries, receiving protections only through the faithful administration of the Emperor's honor by the U.S. trustee.
